…おそらく、自分の「研究」に没頭していて、手を離す気がないのだろう。
それはよくあることなので、彼らは気まぐれな父が降りてくるまでのんびり待つのだった。
contexts.japanesePC: …おそらく、自分の「研究」に没頭していて、手を離す気がないのだろう。
contexts.japanesePS3:
絵羽たちの到着を、源次が金蔵に伝えたはずなのだが、なかなか降りてこない。
…おそらく、自分の「研究」に没頭していて、手を離す気がないのだろう。
それはよくあることなので、彼らは気まぐれな父が降りてくるまでのんびり待つのだった。
contexts.WH: ...He was probably immersed in his own 'research', and couldn't spare the time.
contexts.MG:
Genji had supposedly told Kinzo of Eva's family's arrival, but he still hadn't come down.
...He was probably immersed in his "research" and couldn't spare the time.

findings.sourceReading: The narrator supposes Kinzo is immersed in research and has no intention of stopping it.
findings.alternative: His fickleness is retained in the next sentence and makes disregard for his visitors inferable. The explicit reason nonetheless changes from unwillingness to lack of available time.

findings.description: 国語算数やない becomes “You learn math and language in school, right?” rather than a negation. The contrast with learning an attitude is weakened.

contexts.japanese:
「学校で習うのは国語算数やない。
モノを学ぶ姿勢と態度を学ぶんや。
その基礎ができて、ようやく生涯をかけた勉強が始まるんやで」
「ここをな、勘違いしとるヤツは、生涯学べん石頭や。
国語算数で満点取れても、会社じゃ役に立たへん！」
contexts.japanesePC: 「学校で習うのは国語算数やない。モノを学ぶ姿勢と態度を学ぶんや。その基礎ができて、ようやく生涯をかけた勉強が始まるんやで。」
contexts.japanesePS3:
「学校で習うのは国語算数やない。
モノを学ぶ姿勢と態度を学ぶんや。
その基礎ができて、ようやく生涯をかけた勉強が始まるんやで」
「ここをな、勘違いしとるヤツは、生涯学べん石頭や。
国語算数で満点取れても、会社じゃ役に立たへん！」
contexts.WH: "You learn math and language in school, right?  What you really need to learn is the right attitude for learning more.  Once you form that basis, you can finally start a long period of study that'll last your entire life."
contexts.MG:
"When you're in school, it's not math and language you're learnin'.
What they're really teachin' you is the right outlook and attitude for learnin' more.
Once you've got that base, you can finally start a long period of study that'll last your entire life."
"People who don't get this end up spendin' their whole lives as fools who never learn.
Just gettin' full marks in math and language won't do you any good at your company!"
contexts.UP:
"It's not language or math you learn in school.
What you study is the attitude to have towards studying.
Once you form that basis, you can finally start a long period of study that'll last your entire life."
"People who don't get this will spend the rest of their lives with rocks for brains, totally unable to absorb knowledge.
They might get full marks in math and language, but they'll be useless for their company!"
contexts.note: Both restore negation of language/math as main school purpose and contrast with learning attitude.

findings.sourceReading: Hideyoshi rhetorically says that what one learns in school is not language and arithmetic, but the stance and attitude needed to learn throughout life.
findings.alternative: Schools literally teach those subjects, so the English may look like a sensible paraphrase of his larger argument. The source deliberately uses a forceful negation and places learning attitude within schooling, while the English says it is what one really needs to learn.

findings.description: 男に食わしてもらうため and 貞淑を装う become “dress modestly to entertain men,” replacing economic dependence and a performance of feminine virtue with clothing and entertainment.

contexts.japanese:
「あぁら、これはこれで魅力的よぅ、ねぇ？
時代は変わるのよ。
男に食わしてもらうために貞淑を装わなくてはならなかった時代はとっくに終わってるんだから」
contexts.japanesePC: 「あぁら、これはこれで魅力的よぅ、ねぇ？　時代は変わるのよ。男に食わしてもらうために貞淑を装わなくてはならなかった時代はとっくに終わってるんだから。」
contexts.japanesePS3:
「あぁら、これはこれで魅力的よぅ、ねぇ？
時代は変わるのよ。
男に食わしてもらうために貞淑を装わなくてはならなかった時代はとっくに終わってるんだから」
contexts.WH: "My, isn't that fascinating, right?  Times change.  The time when we had to dress modestly to entertain men ended a long time ago."
contexts.MG:
"Come now, she's quite appealing in her own way, isn't she?
Times change.
The time when we had to act all modest to entertain men ended long ago."

findings.sourceReading: Eva says the era when women had to feign chastity or feminine virtue so that men would support them has long ended. She uses this to defend Jessica’s manner of speaking.
findings.alternative: Modesty overlaps with the virtue she invokes, and the English preserves her claim that times have changed. But 装う here means feign, not dress, and 食わしてもらう means be financially supported, not entertain.
